title: Saying the vow
hookLine: say it before a shrine, a tree, the sky
tomorrow: a whole life of practice in three short words. which three?

cards: Typing sorry is easy. Saying it out loud, to a face, is another thing: the voice shakes, and the words cost something. The Majjhima Nikaya has a story about that cost.

Angulimala is a man the sutta describes as a killer, who met the Buddha and became a monk. On his alms round he sees a woman in a hard, dangerous labor, and it shakes him. He goes back and tells the Buddha.
The Buddha says: go to her, and say one sentence.

teach.b: The sentence is: since I was born, I don't recall knowingly taking the life of any living being; by this truth, may you be well, and your child. Angulimala stops. That would be a lie, he says.
So the Buddha changes the words: since I was born with the noble birth, meaning since he became a monk. Now it's true. He goes, he says it, and the sutta says the woman and her child were well.
Buddhists call this an act of truth, saccakiriya: a true statement, said aloud, as a blessing or a vow. The point isn't magic words. The Buddha wouldn't let him say the sentence until it was true.

That's what saying it aloud does: you can keep a vague hope in your head forever, but your own ears check what your mouth says. It's why people take the precepts aloud, before a monk, a shrine, or just the sky.

And in Theravada communities Angulimala's verse is still chanted for women near childbirth. One for a friend tonight: a blessing for new mothers that rests on a former killer's honesty. Yesterday's vow works the same way.

teach.h: IF A WORD CATCHES, CHANGE IT.
teach.b: If your voice catches on a word, it may not be true yet.
Change it until it is, then say it.

how: Buddhists take the refuges and precepts aloud, often repeating them after a monk or nun or before a home shrine; in Theravada communities the Angulimala verse is chanted as a protection for women near childbirth.

games.q: your sister wants you to say at her graduation dinner that you 'never doubted her for a second.' you did, once, early on. what does Angulimala's story suggest?
o: say it anyway; a kind lie at dinner is harmless.
change the words until they're true, then say them proudly.
say nothing at all, so you can't get it wrong.
games.why: the Buddha didn't cancel Angulimala's blessing; he fixed the sentence until it was true. then it was said, and it carried.

practice: Face a shrine, a window, a tree, or just the sky. Say your vow out loud once, at the volume of an ordinary sentence. If a word catches, change it until it's true and say it again, then rest in the quiet it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Saying the vow: an act of truth, saccakiriya, a true sentence spoken where it can be heard.
